 The Memo Nobody Sent You 
 One day, you're configuring a purchase order in S/4HANA. 
 The next day, there's a little "Ask Joule" button in the corner of your screen. 
 Nobody called a meeting. Nobody sent you a roadmap. The software just... changed. 
 That's what "AI-First" actually looks like on the ground. 
 SAP didn't announce "AI-First, Suite-First" in a press release for fun. This is the defining strategy for everything they build, sell, and invest in — from now through 2026 and beyond. Over 400 embedded AI use cases are live or in flight by end of 2025, across finance, supply chain, HR, procurement, and more. 
 Not as add-ons. Embedded. In the core. 
 And if you're an SAP professional, that changes things — whether you're ready for it or not. 
 So What Does "AI-First" Actually Mean? 
 Let me break it down without the buzzwords. 
 "AI-First" means that when SAP's engineers design a new feature — any feature — AI isn't an afterthought. It's built in from day one. The system learns from your data. It suggests. It predicts. It acts. 
 "Suite-First" means all of this is connected. Joule, SAP's AI copilot, doesn't live in just one product. It moves with you across S/4HANA, SuccessFactors, Ariba, and more. One interface. One context. Your business data flowing through it all. 
 And here's the number that stopped me when I first saw it: in 2024, 7% of companies were using AI as an integral part of their processes. By end of 2025, that number is 29% — and another 51% are actively adopting AI on a project basis. 
 The shift is already happening. The question is where you are in it. 
 The Three Things AI Actually Does to Your Work 
 I keep coming back to three words SAP uses to describe AI's impact on business. 
 Accelerate — AI shortens the gap between having a question and getting an answer. You ask in natural language, you get a result. You stop digging through five menu paths for a number that should take five seconds. 
 Augment — AI gives you capabilities you didn't have before. Not replacing you — giving you superpowers. Predictive demand forecasting that used to require a data science team. Anomaly detection that surfaces problems before they become incidents. 
 Automate — The long tail of repetitive tasks starts running without you. Invoice reconciliation. Approval routing. Periodic reports nobody loved writing anyway. 
 ❓ Now here's the question nobody asks: which of these three is happening to your specific job right now? 
 That answer will shape your next two years more than any certification. 
 Meet the Thing Living Inside Your SAP System 
 You've probably heard of Joule. Maybe you rolled your eyes a little. 
 Fair. There have been a lot of "AI assistants" that turned out to be glorified search bars. 
 Joule is different — not because of the marketing, but because of the architecture. 
 By end of 2025, SAP has 40 Joule Agents running across its portfolio, built on over 2,100 Joule Skills. Not just Joule answering questions. Joule doing things — executing workflows, completing tasks, operating with a level of autonomy that's genuinely new territory for enterprise software. 
 All of this runs on SAP AI Foundation on BTP — the platform SAP calls the "AI operating system" for its entire Business AI portfolio. And underneath that sits Business Data Cloud — a unified, governed data layer that connects SAP and non-SAP data so the AI isn't guessing. It knows your processes. Your history. Your context. 
 When SAP says "relevant, reliable, responsible AI" — this is what makes it relevant. It's grounded in your actual business data, not a generic model of the world. 
 What This Means If You're an SAP Professional Today 
 I'll be straight with you. 
 If your daily work is mostly repetitive execution — running standard reports, processing standard transactions, following standard procedures — AI is coming for that work. Not to fire you. To do those parts faster, so you can do something else. 
 The question is: what is that something else? 
 The SAP professionals I see positioning themselves well right now are the ones shifting from executing the system to shaping the system. They understand what Joule can do. They know where AI recommendations need human judgment. They're the ones who can look at an AI output and say "that's right" or "that's wrong" — and explain why. 
 That ability to critically evaluate AI in a real business context? Joule can't do that for you. That's yours. 
 The Autonomous Enterprise Is the Destination — We're in the Messy Middle 
 SAP calls it the Autonomous Enterprise — a future where processes self-optimize, decisions happen faster, and humans focus on what genuinely requires human thinking. 
 We're not there yet. We're in the messy middle. 
 AI is everywhere but uneven. Powerful but imperfect. Exciting and, if I'm honest, a little disorienting at times. 
 That's exactly why now is the right time to start paying attention — not to become an AI expert, but to become the SAP professional who understands what AI can and can't do, and uses that knowledge to work differently. 
 That's what this series is about. One episode at a time, we'll demystify what AI actually means in the SAP world. Not hype. Not fear. Just an honest look at what's changing, what it means for your work, and what to do about it. 

 Your Turn 
 Which part of your SAP work do you think will be most affected by AI in the next 12 months? Drop a comment — I'm genuinely curious what you're seeing from your corner of the ecosystem. 
 ⏭ Next episode: Meet Joule — and why calling it a "chatbot" completely misses the point.

items.title: Automating SAP SD Material Pricing Using a Rolling 5-Day Market Price Average
items.author: Sneka_E
items.text:
Introduction 
 In SAP Sales and Distribution (SD), the base price of a material is commonly determined using condition type PR00 in the pricing procedure. In some businesses, material prices fluctuate daily based on market rates published by external pricing portals. 
 Maintaining these prices manually can be time-consuming and may result in outdated prices being used during sales order creation. 
 In this blog, I will explain how to automate the PR00 base price calculation in SAP SD using daily high and low market prices, a custom table that retains five days of price history, and a custom pricing routine. 
 1. Business Requirement 
 The business requirement was to calculate the material's base price automatically using market data received from an external portal. The solution needed to meet the following requirements: 
 Fetch the daily high and low prices for relevant products from an external market data source. 
 Store the retrieved prices in SAP on a daily basis using a background job. 
 Retain only the latest five available days of price history for each product. 
 Calculate the average price based on the daily high and low values. 
 Automatically populate condition type PR00 during sales order pricing. 
 Allow users to manually override the calculated price when required. 
 The objective was to reduce manual price maintenance and ensure that the sales order uses a price derived from recent market data. 
 2. Solution Overview 
 The solution consists of two main processes. 
 Process 1: Daily Market Price Update 
 A custom ABAP program retrieves the market prices from the external portal and updates a custom SAP table. A background job executes this program periodically. The table retains five days of price history, while older records are removed automatically. 
 Process 2: Sales Order Price Determination 
 When a user creates a sales order and enters a material, SAP determines the applicable market product code, reads the five-day price history, calculates the average, and returns the result to PR00 through a custom alternative calculation routine. 
 3. Calculating the Daily Market Price 
 The external portal provides the highest and lowest prices for a product for each available pricing date. 
 The daily midpoint is calculated as follows: 
 Daily Mid Price = (Daily High Price + Daily Low Price) / 2 
 For example, consider the following market data for a product. 
 Day High Price Low Price Mid Price 
 Day 1 120 100 110 
 Day 2 130 110 120 
 Day 3 125 105 115 
 Day 4 140 120 130 
 Day 5 135 115 125 
 The five-day average is calculated using the daily midpoint for each of the five days. 
 Five-Day Average = Sum of the five daily midpoints / 5 
 Using the example above: 
 Five-Day Average = (110 + 120 + 115 + 130 + 125) / 5 
 Calculated Base Price = 120 
 This value becomes the proposed base price for the material, subject to the applicable pricing logic. 
 4. Storing Market Prices in SAP 
 A custom ABAP program retrieves the high and low market prices from the external source and stores them in a custom SAP table. 
 The relevant information includes: 
 Product Code: Identifies the product in the external market data feed. 
 Price Date: Identifies the date associated with the market price. 
 High Price: The highest published price for that date. 
 Low Price: The lowest published price for that date. 
 A scheduled background job runs the program to refresh the market data. The custom table retains the latest five available days of history for each product, and older records are deleted automatically. 
 This approach keeps the data required for price calculation readily available in SAP without maintaining an unlimited history in the operational table. 
 5. Mapping SAP Materials to Market Products 
 The SAP material number and the external market product code may follow different naming conventions. Therefore, SAP needs a mapping mechanism to identify the correct market data for each material. 
 When a material is entered in the sales order, the custom pricing logic derives the relevant material identifier and uses the configured mapping rules to determine the corresponding external product code. 
 The system then retrieves the price records associated with that product code. 
 In scenarios where a material's price depends on multiple market products, the applicable business formula must also be determined from the mapping configuration. 
 This mapping step is essential because selecting the wrong product code would result in an incorrect base price, even if the average calculation itself is correct. 
 6. Implementing the Logic in SAP SD Pricing 
 The automatic calculation is implemented using a custom VOFM alternative calculation routine assigned to condition type PR00 in the relevant pricing procedure. 
 The high-level implementation steps are: 
 1. Identify the sales document types and pricing procedure for which automatic pricing is required. 
 2. Configure the material-to-market-product mapping and the applicable calculation rules. 
 3. Read the latest five available price records for the relevant product code from the custom table. 
 4. Calculate the daily midpoint using the high and low values for each date. 
 5. Calculate the five-day average of the daily midpoints. 
 6. Apply any additional product-specific calculation rules, where applicable. 
 7. Return the calculated amount to PR00 during sales order pricing. 
 The routine is assigned to the alternative calculation type field for PR00 in pricing procedure configuration (transaction V/08). 
 As a result, the base price is calculated during sales order pricing rather than requiring the user to maintain it manually for every order. 
 7. Sales Order Processing 
 Once the configuration and routine are in place, the process works as follows: 
 1. The background job refreshes the market price data in SAP. 
 2. The user creates a sales order and enters the relevant material. 
 3. SAP determines the pricing procedure and processes condition type PR00. 
 4. The custom routine identifies the market product code and reads the required price history. 
 5. SAP calculates the five-day average and populates PR00 with the resulting price. 
 6. The user reviews the proposed price and can manually override it if permitted by the condition configuration. 
 7. The sales order is saved, and subsequent delivery and billing processes continue according to the existing configuration. 
 8. Important Considerations 
 When implementing a similar solution, the following points should be validated: 
 Data availability: Define what should happen if fewer than five valid daily price records are available. 
 Price freshness: Ensure the background job completes successfully before the price is required for sales order creation. 
 Product mapping: Validate that each relevant SAP material maps to the correct external product code. 
 Currency and unit of measure: Confirm that market prices and SAP condition values use compatible currencies and units, or apply the necessary conversions. 
 Rounding: Align the calculation precision and rounding rules with the business requirement. 
 Error handling: Define the expected behaviour when market data is missing, invalid, or unavailable. 
 Manual override: Confirm whether users are allowed to change the calculated PR00 value and how subsequent pricing recalculations should behave. 
 These checks help ensure that the automation remains reliable when market data or business conditions change. 
 Conclusion 
 Automating material pricing in SAP SD can reduce manual effort and improve the consistency of sales order pricing when market prices change frequently. 
 By combining a scheduled market data update, a custom price history table, a rolling five-day average calculation, and a VOFM alternative calculation routine for PR00, SAP can determine the base price automatically during sales order creation. 
 The key to a successful implementation is not only the average calculation, but also reliable market data integration, correct material mapping, appropriate pricing configuration, and clear handling of exceptions.

items.title: Customizing Tendering E-Mail Content in SAP Transportation Management
items.author: Rajashiva_Ramalingam
items.text:
During tendering, SAP TM e-mails carriers at each step: when a freight RFQ is published, when a quotation is awarded or rejected, and when tendering is canceled. The texts SAP delivers for these messages are generic. Most projects want to change the wording and add information from their own freight orders that the standard e-mail does not carry. 
 This blog shows how to do both. Changing the text is customizing: you copy the standard SE61 documents to Z versions and assign them to the tendering events. Filling the text with your own data is done in the BAdI /SCMTMS/TEND_SEND_EMAILS, where REPLACE_TEXT_SYMBOL gives every placeholder its value and GET_TEXT can extend the finished message. The examples come from our own implementation.

items.title: Schedule line category not redetermining after custom code changes item category value on sales orde
items.author: Joanna1998
items.text:
Hey guys! 
 Requirement is: if user manually changes plant (VBAP-WERKS) on sales order or the system changes plant based on ABC process (not enough stock in one plant, so system changes to another plant), then change item category value (VBAP-PSTYV). Item category should be derived from custom table. 
 We put our code in USEREXIT_MOVE_F8ELD_TO_VBAP and the code works fine when the user changes the plant. 
 But the problem is with ABC process. The ABC/ATP does not retrigger once the item category is changed in userexit. And the ABC/ATP process happens only for 'old' item category value and determines schedule line category only for old PSTYV. I debugged and saw that old schedule line is stored in MVERF structures. Even though the correct schedule line is derived later on in the code based on FM rv_scheduling _type_ determine, it gets later on overwritten with old schedule line values stored in MVERF. 
 Any ideas how to solve this would be highly appreciated, thank you

deep_dives.title: Debugging a CAP draftActivate hang on HANA Cloud
deep_dives.explanation:
The report: POST .../VendorRequests(ID=...,IsActiveEntity=false)/draftActivate never returns on HANA Cloud (free tier, @sap/cds 10.1.1, @cap-js/hana 3.1.1), but works on SQLite. The log ends at the CREATE of the active entity. The model has VendorRequests with @odata.draft.enabled and a Composition of many RequestDocuments, whose `content` is a `LargeBinary` with `@Core.MediaType`. The author has ruled out custom handlers, M_BLOCKED_TRANSACTIONS is empty, and redeployment did not help. The root cause is not confirmed, because the final test result is an empty placeholder.

A practical approach is to bisect. Activate a draft with no document rows, then one with an empty or tiny binary, then a larger one. If only the binary case hangs, the problem is LOB handling in the INSERT path and not the draft logic. Also test a draft with documents but without the content value, to separate the composition insert from the LOB insert.

On the HANA side, look at the statement while it hangs: `M_ACTIVE_STATEMENTS`, `M_CONNECTIONS`, and the lock views (`M_TRANSACTION_LOCKS`, `M_LOCKS`). An empty `M_BLOCKED_TRANSACTIONS` rules out a lock wait but not an idle connection or a stalled driver. Also check whether the free-tier instance is stopped or short of memory. These are checks, not conclusions: the post does not establish which applies.

Two more questions are open: whether the composition children are inserted in the same transaction as the parent, and whether the hybrid profile (`cds watch --profile hybrid` with `cds bind`) behaves the same when deployed. Report any result with the exact versions.

deep_dives.title: Late item category changes and the SD item processing sequence
deep_dives.explanation:
The poster derives VBAP-PSTYV from VBAP-WERKS in a custom table, inside USEREXIT_MOVE_F8ELD_TO_VBAP. For a manual plant change this works. For ABC/ATP plant reassignment it does not: the ATP check does not re-run after PSTYV changes, and the schedule line category is still derived for the original item category.

The poster traced the cause to old schedule line values held in MVERF, which overwrite the corrected schedule line that FM `RV_SCHEDULING_TYPE_DETERMINE` derives later. So the root problem is ordering: availability and schedule line data are already built when the item category changes.

The post gives no solution. Directions to evaluate (not confirmed by the post): check whether the change can move earlier, to where the plant is set by ABC; use standard item category determination and its customizing instead of a userexit; or force schedule line redetermination after the change. Each should be tested in the debugger with an ABC case and a manual case, watching MVERF and the schedule line table before and after.

deep_dives.title: Designing MCP tools over OData: what the excerpts leave open
deep_dives.explanation:
Part 1 exposes the Business Partner (A2X) API as an MCP server on SAP Integration Suite, deployed to Integration Cell and published through Developer Hub. Part 2 connects Joule Work Desktop as client. A third post exposes standard SAP tables as tools for custom agents. None of the excerpts show tool definitions, authentication or limits.

For an ABAP team, the design questions are familiar. A tool needs a clear description, typed inputs and a bounded output. Raw table access needs a restricted field list, a row cap and an authorisation check on the end user, not a technical user. A CDS view or released API is a better surface than a table because it can carry access control (DCL) and a defined projection.

Also keep in mind that clients differ in which MCP capabilities they render. One poster asks whether Joule Work Desktop displays prompts from `prompts/list`, which is unanswered. Test the server with an MCP inspector, independent of the client.

interview_questions.question: A CAP draft-enabled entity activates on SQLite but hangs on HANA Cloud at the INSERT of the active entity. How do you investigate?
interview_questions.answer: First, reproduce with a minimal payload and bisect: no child rows, child rows without the binary field, then small and large binaries. This separates draft logic from LOB handling, since a LargeBinary field was the suspect in the report. Then look at HANA while the request hangs: M_ACTIVE_STATEMENTS and M_CONNECTIONS for the statement, and M_TRANSACTION_LOCKS or M_LOCKS for lock waits. An empty M_BLOCKED_TRANSACTIONS rules out a simple lock wait only. Check that the instance is running and not out of memory, especially on a free tier. Confirm that the same versions of @sap/cds and @cap-js/hana are used everywhere. Only after that would I suspect the driver or the framework and raise an issue with the minimal reproduction.

interview_questions.question: A userexit changes the item category (PSTYV) on a sales order item when the plant changes. It works for manual changes but not for ABC plant reassignment. Why might that happen and how would you approach it?
interview_questions.answer: The likely cause is sequence. ABC/ATP runs with the original item category, so availability and schedule line data are built for it. The userexit then changes PSTYV, but ATP does not re-run. The poster found that stale values in MVERF overwrite the schedule line category later determined by RV_SCHEDULING_TYPE_DETERMINE. I would confirm this in the debugger by comparing a manual and an ABC case, watching MVERF and the schedule line data at each step. Then I would consider moving the logic earlier, using standard item category determination customizing instead of the userexit, or forcing redetermination after the change. I would not assume any of these works without testing, as the thread has no confirmed fix.

interview_questions.question: You are asked to expose S/4HANA data to an LLM agent through MCP. What design rules do you apply?
interview_questions.answer: Expose a bounded, described tool and not a raw table. Each tool needs a clear description, typed inputs and a limited output with a row cap. Prefer a released API or a CDS view with access control over a table, so the projection and authorisation are explicit. Execute on behalf of the end user so that authorisation objects apply, not through a broad technical user. Restrict returned fields to what the use case needs. Log the calls. Test the server independently of the client with an MCP inspector, as clients differ in which capabilities they render. The posts today do not show how their patterns handle these points, so they must be checked before reuse.
